prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: [val2][adversarial] Incident IDs vs prose (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Incident" · longest unbreakable word 68px · one-line width 127px
  col 2: header "Trace ID" · longest unbreakable word 245px · one-line width 245px
  col 3: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 52px · one-line width 52px
  col 4: header "Summary" · longest unbreakable word 65px · one-line width 612px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 735px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 734px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"Severity takes as much space as the longer fields, leaving the summary narrow and forcing the longest trace ID to break."},"B":{"grade":"poor","why":"The trace IDs stay intact and the summaries read well, but every incident ID breaks across three lines, making identification and comparison difficult."},"C":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Trace IDs stay intact and the summaries have reasonable room, but every incident ID breaks across two lines."},"D":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Both identifier columns stay intact, severity has sufficient space, and the summaries wrap into manageable lines with consistent row rhythm."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"Incident IDs stay intact and the summaries have generous space, but the longest trace ID breaks across two lines."}},"best":["D"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"The trade-off between preserving the longest trace ID and giving the summaries more space is close; D keeps both identifier types intact while retaining readable summaries."}
